title: Ibn Jubayr's pilgrimage
hookLine: an Andalusian's Hajj journal, full of wonder at Mecca
tomorrow: how do you describe a place that feels nothing like home?

cards: Phones fill up with photos nobody looks at twice: the same sunset forty times, a blurry crowd, a plate of food. Ibn Jubayr, a secretary from al-Andalus, had no camera on his Hajj, so he wrote.
His journal runs in dated entries, like a diary, and when he reaches Mecca the entries slow down and fill with light: lamps, crowds, the house at the center.

teach.b: There's a story told about why he went: a ruler he served pressed wine on him, and he set out to make amends. Later writers tell it; his journal doesn't explain itself. What the journal does is look.
He describes the Kaaba in its cloth, the sanctuary lit by lamps and candles at night, people from many lands circling together, the water of Zamzam drawn and shared.
And again and again he admits that words fall short. That's the surprise of a pilgrim's journal: the writer's skill keeps running out, and he keeps writing anyway.
He isn't trying to impress anyone, and he doesn't pretend to have it all figured out. He's trying to keep a day of wonder from slipping away.
The Qur'an calls the house a place people return to, in Pickthall: “And when We made the House (at Makka) a resort for mankind and a sanctuary.” A resort: somewhere people keep coming back.
Ibn Jubayr wrote so that he could come back too, by reading. The senses hold a day better than a summary does: light on stone, the taste of the water, many languages praying in one place.

how: Pilgrims returning from Hajj often share what they saw with family and friends; some keep journals, a habit with a long history in Muslim travel writing.

games.q: your grandmother tells you about the day she got married, and you want to keep it. what fits Ibn Jubayr?
o: write it down soon, with what she saw and heard that day.
trust that you'll remember the main points later.
only write it down if she can give exact dates.
games.why: the journal keeps the senses: light, water, crowds. that's what brings a day back when you read it again.

practice: Take paper and a pen. Write down one moment of wonder from this past week, with what you saw, heard, smelled or tasted, not what it meant. Keep writing slowly for the whole sit, even if it's only a few lines.
